articles.title: Which NTS test do you need?
lines: NTS (National Testing Service) runs several different tests. Check your university's admission notice or the job advertisement to see which one applies to you.
## NAT: National Aptitude Test

For admission after intermediate (12 years of education) or after a bachelor's (14 years). There is a separate paper for each group of study. This app covers four 12-year papers: NAT-IE (Pre-Engineering), NAT-IM (Pre-Medical), NAT-ICS (Computer Science) and NAT-IA (Arts).
## GAT General: Graduate Assessment Test
Usually needed for MS, MPhil and PhD admission. It tests English, analytical and quantitative reasoning, with no subject section.
## Recruitment tests

NTS also tests candidates for jobs. Each employer sets its own syllabus and pattern, usually a mix of English, maths, analytical reasoning, general knowledge, Islamic Studies and Pakistan Studies, and often a job-related subject. The Recruitment tests here follow a typical mix.
Patterns can change. Your own test notice and roll number slip always come first.

articles.title: Test patterns at a glance
lines: ## NAT (12 years of education)
90 questions in 120 minutes, according to the pattern published by NTS.
- English 20: sentence completion 5, analogy 3, antonym 4, comprehension 5, synonym 3
- Analytical 20: scenario-based 12, statement-based 8
- Quantitative 20: arithmetic 13, algebra 4, geometry 3
- Subject 30: depends on your group
- NAT-IE: Physics 10, Chemistry 10, Mathematics 10
- NAT-IM: Physics 8, Chemistry 8, Biology 14
- NAT-ICS: Physics 10, Mathematics 10, Computer 10
- NAT-IA: Islamiyat or Ethics 10, Pakistan Studies 10, General Knowledge 10
## GAT General
Commonly described as 100 questions in 120 minutes: about 35 verbal, 35 analytical and 30 quantitative. This split comes from preparation sources, not from NTS, so confirm it in your notice.
## Recruitment (typical)
100 questions in 120 minutes in this app: English 25, Quantitative 20, Analytical 15, General Knowledge 15, Islamic Studies or Ethics 15, Pakistan Studies 10.
## Negative marking
Preparation sources report no negative marking on NAT and GAT, and this app does not deduct marks. If your notice says otherwise, skip the questions you cannot narrow down.

articles.title: An eight-week plan
lines: ## Weeks 1 and 2: find your level
- Take one full test under real timing, before you study anything
- Read the results by section and list your three weakest topics
- Start a vocabulary notebook: ten new words a day
## Weeks 3 to 6: build skills
- Practise one weak topic a day in short sets
- Read every explanation, even for questions you got right
- Take one full test each week, and spend as long reviewing it as you spent sitting it
- Revise maths rules: percentages, ratios, averages, speed and work
## Weeks 7 and 8: test practice
- Take two or three full tests a week at the same time of day as your real test
- Stop learning new topics in the last three days
- Sleep properly the night before

articles.title: Only two weeks left?
lines: - Take one full test on the first day to find where the easiest marks are
- English and analytical reasoning usually improve fastest with practice, so start there
- For group subjects, revise key formulas and definitions instead of reading whole chapters
- Take a full test every second day and review it the same day
- Practise the weakest topic for 30 minutes each day

articles.title: Managing your time
lines: A 90-question paper in 120 minutes gives you about 80 seconds a question. A 100-question paper gives you 72 seconds.
- Do the questions you find easy first, then come back to the rest
- If a question takes more than two minutes, mark it and move on
- Scenario puzzles take longer: draw a quick table before you start
- Keep the last ten minutes to go back to marked questions
- With no negative marking, never leave a question blank: rule out what you can and choose

articles.title: Before and during the test
lines: ## The day before
- Read your roll number slip closely: date, reporting time, centre and what to bring
- Visit or look up the centre so that you know the route
- Keep your documents ready, including your CNIC or the ID the slip asks for
## On the day
- Reach the centre early
- Do not take in anything the slip forbids, such as a phone or calculator
- Read the instructions on the paper and answer sheet before you start
## On a bubble sheet
- Fill each bubble completely and firmly, as the instructions say
- After every few questions, check that the question number matches the bubble row
- If you skip a question, leave its row empty so later answers stay in line

articles.title: English
lines: ## Sentence completion
- Cover the options, and guess the word from the sentence
- Look for signal words: although, because, however, therefore
- With two blanks, rule options out using one blank at a time
## Analogies
- Make a sentence linking the first pair: 'a pen is used for writing'
- Try the same sentence on each option
## Synonyms and antonyms
- Learn word roots and prefixes: mal- is bad, ben- is good, -cide is killing
- For antonyms, first decide what the word means, then look for its opposite. A common trap is a synonym in the options
## Comprehension
- Read the question first, then the passage
- The answer must come from the passage, not from what you already know
- Beware of options that are true in general but not stated in the text

articles.title: Analytical reasoning
lines: ## Scenario questions
- Turn the rules into a small table or diagram before reading the questions
- Note what must be true, and what only could be true
- For 'if' questions, make a fresh copy of your diagram
## Statement questions
- Find the conclusion first, then ask what it depends on
- An assumption is what the argument needs but does not say
- For syllogisms, draw circles and test whether the conclusion must follow, not just whether it could
## Series and codes
- Check differences first, then ratios, then alternate terms
- Write the alphabet with its numbers at the top of your rough work

articles.title: Quantitative
lines: - Calculators are generally not allowed, so practise mental arithmetic
- Learn squares to 20, cubes to 10, and common fractions as percentages
- Estimate first: often only one option is close
- Use the options: put them into the problem when algebra looks long
- Convert units before calculating
- In percentage questions, take care with what the percentage is 'of'
- Draw a quick sketch for every geometry question

articles.title: Science and computer subjects
lines: - Questions come mostly from intermediate textbooks, so revise from your own books
- Keep a one-page formula sheet for Physics and Mathematics
- In Chemistry, know trends in the periodic table and common reaction types
- In Biology, expect many direct questions, so definitions and diagrams from the textbook pay off
- In Computer, practise tracing short programs by hand and writing basic SQL

articles.title: General Knowledge, Islamic and Pakistan Studies
lines: - Recruitment tests often include current affairs. This app avoids facts that go out of date, so also follow the news in the months before your test
- Learn the key dates of the Pakistan Movement in order
- Know the main features of the 1956, 1962 and 1973 constitutions
- For Islamic Studies, revise the five pillars, the main events of the Seerah and the basics of the Holy Quran
- Non-Muslim candidates are usually offered Ethics. Check your notice
